Introduction

Aviation accounted for 593 Mt of CO2 emissions in 2018, representing 2% of global and 12% of transport-related emissions.1 With growing air travel, fuel consumption is expected to rise up to 2.6-fold by 2050, making net-zero emissions imperative to tackle aviation’s environmental impact.1,2 However, aviation’s reliance on energy-dense liquid fuels and long-lived aircraft makes decarbonization particularly challenging.1,2 Despite improvements in flight efficiency, carbon intensity of aviation has stagnated due to continued fossil-based jet-fuel dependency.2,3 Thus, replacing conventional aviation fuel with non-fossil-sourced sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is a crucial step in pursuing the emission abatement by 2050.1,3,4

A key step to accelerate SAF deployment is identifying renewable feedstocks capable of delivering hydrocarbons beyond linear n- and iso-alkanes, which are dominant in currently established SAF pathways—such as alcohol-to-jet synthetic paraffinic kerosene (ATJ-SPK)5 and hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids synthetic paraffinic kerosene (HEFA-SPK).6,7 A fully drop-in SAF must also include 30%–50% of cyclic hydrocarbons, namely naphthenes and aromatics, to maintain energy density and ensure engine compatibility.3,8,9 In this context, naphthenes represent an attractive alternative, as they can provide the required fuel performance while mitigating the environmental drawbacks associated with aromatics—such as soot and contrail formation.3,10,11

Among renewable feedstocks, lignin, a natural and renewable carbon source available worldwide as constituent of lignocellulosic biomass (LCB), has attracted significant attention as a sustainable precursor for producing naphthenes suitable for SAF application.12,13,14,15,16 Lignin is a branched bio-polymer, mainly composed of repeating phenylpropanoid units, connected by ether (C–O–C) and carbon-carbon (C–C) inter-unit linkages.17,18,19,20 The intrinsic phenolic structure, composition (average C10), and natural abundance make this raw material an ideal precursor for supplying cyclic SAF components.12,13,14,15

In recent years, lignin valorization has gained renewed momentum through the development of lignin-first strategies.21,22 These pathways yield lignin streams that are more amenable to further valorization compared to technical lignins generated through conventional LCB processing.20,21,22,23 Among lignin-first approaches, reductive catalytic fractionation (RCF) has emerged as one of the most widespread strategies.24,25,26,27,28,29 RCF enables the production of highly processable, low-molecular-weight (MW) refined lignin oil (RLO), primarily composed of monomers and dimers, along with some trimers and larger oligomers, by introducing catalytic stabilization during lignin extraction and depolymerization.29,30,31,32,33,34 However, the high content of oxygenated moieties in lignin oil necessitates further upgrading to align with SAF specifications. In this context, catalytic hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) has been explored as an effective strategy to convert lignin oils into non-oxygenated fuel.13,15,35,36

HDO of lignin oil has been investigated in recent years, demonstrating the efficient production of SAF-range cyclic hydrocarbons.37,38,39,40,41,42,43,44 Stone et al. reported the upgrading of lignin oil via continuous catalytic HDO into a mixture enriched in C9–C20 alkylated aromatics ideal for SAF.39 Cao et al. successfully transformed lignin oil into a blend predominantly composed of C6–C10 and C14–C20 liquid hydrocarbons.41 Webber et al. upgraded lignin oil into an aromatic-rich blend with the jet-range distillate dominated by C9 alkylbenzenes.42 The products were blended at 25 vol % with paraffinic SAFs (HEFA-SPK and ATJ-SPK), meeting all the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) D7566 specifications.42

Our recent study highlighted the direct influence of lignin oil physicochemical properties on both HDO efficiency and selectivity.43 The work emphasized the importance of selecting an appropriate biorefining strategy for efficient HDO, positioning lignin oil derived from RCF as a superior feedstock compared to technical lignin, largely due to its lower average MW.43 In addition, variations in the content of oxygenated end-units (γ-OH) in lignin-derived molecules were shown to influence carbon retention during HDO, thereby directly affecting the composition of the resulting fuel slate.43 This study underscores a key relationship between the chemical composition of lignin oil and the carbon range in the resulting SAF blend, building upon previous works.45,46,47

Taken together, these findings highlight the need for detailed structure-performance studies to advance the understanding of how specific molecular features, and distinct molecular families, such as monomers, dimers, and larger oligomers, govern HDO behavior and contribute to the final SAF blend. This area remains largely unexplored, as the inherent structural complexity of lignin oil has so far confined such studies to the use of simplified model compounds.48,49,50,51,52,53

Model-compound studies have provided important mechanistic insight, particularly for monomers and selected dimers. As example, Lercher et al. investigated HDO of a representative mixture of lignin-derived C6–C9 monomers and common ether-linked dimers (β-O-4, α-O-4, and 4-O-5) and C–C linked dimers (5-5, β-1, and β-β).51 Generally, lignin-derived monomers retained their carbon backbone into C6–C9 mono-naphthenes, ether-linked dimers underwent C–O bond cleavage into mono-naphthenes, while unsubstituted C–C linked dimers did not undergo hydrocracking, producing mostly C12, C14, and C16 bi-naphthenes.51 Similarly, Zhang et al. reported selective formation of C6–C9 naphthenes from lignin-derived monomers and conversion of ether-linked dimers into mono-naphthenes, while non-alkylated 5-5 dimers preserved the carbon skeleton into yield C12 naphthenes after HDO.52 Salam et al. further examined dimer HDO and showed that C–C bond cleavage can also occur for 5-5 motifs under more severe conditions, yielding C6 products and evidencing hydrocracking.53

Despite their value, model systems cannot represent real feedstock behavior relevant to SAF-oriented HDO, which remains underexplored due to its inherent complexity. Unlike synthetically pure monomers or dimers, RCF lignin oil is a complex mixture of monomers, dimers, trimers, and larger oligomers, present in varying concentrations and bearing a wide range of end-units and inter-unit linkages. Importantly, most model dimer studies focus on non-substituted, structurally simplified ether-linked dimers, which represent only a minor fraction of RCF-derived lignin dimers. By contrast, RCF lignin oils are enriched in C–C linked dimers that are typically alkylated and often feature substitution not only on the aromatic ring but also along the inter-unit linkage itself. These additional degrees of structural variation not captured by model compounds can strongly influence reactivity, carbon retention, and product distribution under HDO conditions, ultimately shaping the SAF-range hydrocarbon slate. Nevertheless, the presence of trimers, tetramers, and larger oligomers in real lignin oil raises a critical question regarding their contribution to the formation of SAF-range naphthenes during HDO.

To address the intrinsic structural complexity of lignin-derived feedstocks, fractionation has emerged in recent years as powerful downstream processing method.54,55,56 In general, those feedstocks can be separated using distillation,57,58,59 liquid-liquid chromatography,60,61 liquid-liquid extraction,62,63,64 solvent-based fractionation,65,66,67,68,69,70 and membrane separation.71,72,73,74 In particular, solvent-based fractionation has been exploited as a mean to separate lignin feedstocks into fractions with varying structural and physicochemical properties, enabling in-depth structural analysis,65,69,75,76 structure-performance relationship studies,68,70 and the selective application of lignin-derived molecules.38,67,77,78

Seminal work by Van Aelst et al. employed solvent-based fractionation as a key tool to enable detailed structural investigation of lignin oil derived from RCF of pine wood.75 The lignin oil was separated into six structurally less-complex fractions, more amendable for chemical analysis, using mixtures of n-heptane and ethyl acetate. Notably, this approach enabled the unambiguous assignment of over 80% of the inter-unit linkages (β-5, β-1, β-β,5-5, β-O-4) and aliphatic end-units (4-P-γ-OH, 4-P, 4-E, 4-P-γ-OMe, 4-M, 4-propenol) present in the original lignin oil by 2D heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) NMR.75 Building on this approach, Dao Thi and Van Aelst et al. applied identical RCF conditions and subsequent fractionation protocol to pine wood, enabling cumulative identification and quantification across all fractions of 11 monomers (34 wt %), 36 dimers (16 wt %), and 21 trimers (7 wt %) using two-dimensional gas chromatography equipped with a flame ionization detector and mass spectrometer (GC×GC-MS/FID).76 Complementary studies have further demonstrated that solvent-based fractionation enables meaningful structure-performance correlations across different lignin feedstocks.68,69,70

Beyond structural elucidation, fractionation has also been shown to directly support catalytic upgrading of lignin feedstocks toward aviation-relevant hydrocarbons. Huang et al. demonstrated a lignin-first biorefining strategy in which apple wood was catalytically depolymerized over Ru/SiC, followed by hexane fractionation to isolate a monomer-rich lignin oil fraction.78 The fraction subsequently underwent HDO in a fixed-bed reactor over MoO3 catalyst at 360°C to produce aromatics hydrocarbons in the C7–C12 range, suitable for aviation.78 Similarly, Verma et al. employed solvent-based fractionation (n-heptane/ethyl acetate) of birch-derived RCF lignin oil to generate feedstocks enriched in lignin-derived monomers and dimers.38 Upon aqueous-phase HDO over Ru/C, these enriched fractions were selectively converted into C7–C9 mono-naphthenes and C14–C16 bi-naphthenes, closely matching the desired SAF carbon-number distribution.38

Despite the valuable insights provided by prior studies, the specific roles played by the diverse molecular components within lignin oil fractions in producing targeted hydrocarbons remain poorly understood. Addressing this gap requires a systematic investigation of lignin oil structural motifs to deepen structure-performance understanding under real-feed HDO conditions. In particular, this entails (1) elucidating how monomers and dimers convert during HDO and how structural variations influence product distribution, and (2) assessing whether larger species, such as trimers and higher oligomers, can contribute to the formation of SAF-range hydrocarbons.

This study therefore aims to establish a detailed molecular-level understanding of how individual components in lignin oil convert during HDO with the goal of identifying which specific RLO molecules, monomers, dimers, or larger oligomers serve as precursors to HDO products. To this end, solvent-based fractionation is employed to divide RCF lignin oil into well-defined subfractions that are individually subjected to HDO. By correlating the resulting product profiles with the structural features imposed by RCF chemistry, particularly within monomeric and dimeric species, this study clarifies how molecular structure governs reactivity and product selectivity. The carbon backbone of each precursor is used as a key descriptor to track its transformation into SAF-range naphthenes. Additionally, the contribution of trimers and larger oligomers to the final SAF blend is explicitly evaluated. Collectively, these structure-product relationships provide a foundation for rational optimization of lignin-to-SAF conversion pathways.

Results and discussion

RCF and fractionation of lignin oil: Composition and properties

Initially, pine wood (softwood) was selected as RCF feedstock due to its dominance of guaiacyl units, resulting in an RLO containing a higher amount of dimers and oligomers than other feedstocks, such as poplar or eucalyptus (hardwood).34,75 Additionally, Ru/C was selected as a catalyst due to its elevated deoxygenating activity during RCF, which provides minimal oxygenated end-unit functionalities (i.e., low γ-OH content).43,79 Therefore, RLO was generated via RCF processing of pine wood over Ru/C catalyst at 235°C, with 30 bars of H2, for 3 h in methanol (MeOH), as described in section A.2 of the supplemental information.75,79,80,81 Subsequently, the RLO was divided into six subfractions using a sequential solvent-based fractionation with heptane and ethyl acetate (EtOAc) as solvents, as described in section A.3 of the supplemental information.75,76 Accordingly, those subfractions are noted as H100 (100% heptane), H80 (80% heptane/20% EtOAc), H60 (60% heptane/40% EtOAc), H40 (40%heptane/60% EtOAc), H20 (20% heptane/80% EtOAc), and E100 (100% EtOAc). Overall, the sequential solvent-based fractionation subdivided 30 g of pristine RLO in its respective fractions—referred to as H100 through E100—with a cumulative mass of around 28.5 g. In addition to the six fractions, the process generated a solid residue weighing about 0.5 g. As a result, the total mass recovered after the process amounted to 29 g, corresponding to approximately 97 wt % of the initial RLO (30 g). The reader is referred to section A.3 of the supplemental information for further details and more information regarding the RLO weight-distribution throughout the six fractions, specifically reported in Scheme S1, Table S1, and Figure S1.

Before being employed as a feedstock for HDO, each isolated subfraction, as well as the RLO, was characterized using gel permeation chromatography (GPC), GC×GC-MS/FID, and with 1H–13C HSQC NMR and 31P NMR spectroscopy, as described in sections A.5, A.6, and A.7 of the supplemental information. The fractionation process allows the molecular components of the parent RLO to be distributed among the fractions, both qualitatively, in terms of the types of monomers, dimers, and oligomers, and quantitatively, in terms of their respective yields. From a size perspective, the earliest fractions contain the smallest molecules, primarily monomers and dimers, whereas the later fractions are enriched in oligomers. This trend is confirmed by the GPC chromatograms, which show a progressive increase in MW from fraction H100 to E100 (see supplemental notes section B.1 in the supplemental information, Figure S2, and Table S1). These results are consistent with previous reports.75,76

For a detailed molecular insight, the identification and quantification of the lignin-derived monomers and dimers were performed using GC×GC for the individual fractions as well as the original RLO. As expected, the monomer content decreased across these fractions from H100 to E100, as displayed in Figure 1. Notably, the most abundant monomer in H100 is 4-propyl guaiacol, accounting for 52 wt %. By contrast, 4-propanol guaiacol is the most abundant monomer in H80 and H60, with contents of 17.6 and 11.2 wt %, respectively.

The structures of all the identified monomers are provided in Scheme S3, whereas a full overview of the monomer distribution across the fractions is shown in Figure S6 and Table S4. Although the lignin feedstock is derived from softwood and is therefore expected to consist predominantly of G-type units, trace amounts of S- and H-type monomers were detected in selected fractions. Their presence is likely attributable to minor cross-contamination in the original material, which becomes detectable after fractionation. The high resolving power of the fractionation process concentrates minor components, thereby amplifying and revealing trace impurities that would otherwise remain below the detection limit in the bulk sample.

In terms of dimer content (Figure 2), a peaked distribution was observed across the fractions, with H60 exhibiting the highest dimer abundance, followed by H80, H40, H100, and H20, whereas E100 contained only negligible amounts of dimers. Moreover, the distribution of dimers varies depending on their structural type. Compared to monomers, dimer structures are significantly more complex. For this reason, dimers are herein classified according to their C–C inter-unit linkages (I-ULs) into four characteristic types: β-5, β-1, β-β, and 5-5 (Figure 2). In addition to these most abundant dimers, a category of “others” was included, representing a minor subset of molecules primarily composed of dimers with ethers C–O I-UL—specifically, 4-O-5 and β-O-4—as well as the native I-UL phenyl coumaran, which is a direct precursor to β-5.75

Among the identified dimeric species, β-5 I-UL linkages were the most prevalent across all fractions, with the highest abundance observed in the intermediate fractions (notably H60 and H80), while only minor contributions were detected in H20 and E100 (Figure 2). In addition, β-1 linked dimers represented the second most abundant family, following a similar distribution trend across the fractions. Furthermore, 5-5 linked dimers were preferentially enriched in the lighter fractions H100, H80, and H60, whereas their contribution decreased markedly in heavier fractions. By contrast, β-β linked dimers were present at lower overall levels and were mostly concentrated in the heavy fraction H40 and absent in the first fraction H100. Additional minor dimeric structures, grouped as others, were detected primarily in the monomer- and dimer-enriched fractions while being negligible in the heavier fractions. The specific distribution of all the identified dimers across different fractions and their corresponding structures is presented in Tables S5–S13 of the supplemental information. It is important to mention that most identified dimers exhibit strong C–C bonds that cannot be easily broken during HDO, while only a portion possess ether linkages that can be easily cleaved during HDO.

To better understand the molecular variability across the fractions, 1H–13C HSQC NMR analysis was performed to identify and quantify various end-units (EUs) and I-UL across the six fractions as well as the original RLO. A clear trend was observed: the content of EU decreases from H100 to E100, primarily due to a declining proportion of monomeric species. Conversely, I-ULs progressively increase across the fractions, reflecting the enrichment of high-MW molecules in the later fractions. Importantly, beyond what can be accessed by GPC and GC×GC, 1H–13C HSQC NMR provides molecular-level insights into larger structures such as trimers and tetramers, particularly enriched in H60 and H40, as well as even larger oligomers predominantly present in H20 and E100. A detailed breakdown of the different EUs is presented in Figure S3 and Table S2, while the I-ULs are detailed in Figure S4 and Table S3. In addition, all EU and I-UL structures have been assigned based on 1H-13C HSQC NMR analysis, and the corresponding spectra with peak assignments are provided in Scheme S2.

To further rationalize the polarity differences across the fractions, quantitative hydroxyl group analysis was performed by 31P NMR. A clear increase in aliphatic OH content (mmol g−1) was observed from H100 to E100, indicating a progressive enrichment of oxygenated functionalities across the fractions. This trend is consistent with the increasing abundance of oxygen-containing inter-unit linkages revealed by 1H–13C HSQC NMR and reflects the higher polarity of the heavier fractions. The corresponding 31P NMR data are reported in Figure S5. For comprehensive discussion and better interpretation of the analytics, see supplemental notes, section B.2 of the supplemental information.

Effect of catalyst type on HDO performance and product selectivity

Prior to investigating the HDO of the six subfractions derived from the RLO, a catalyst screening was conducted to evaluate the influence of different hydrogenation catalysts on HDO performance and product distribution. These experiments were performed using the full RLO as a representative feedstock under HDO conditions that were subsequently applied throughout the manuscript, namely 300°C, 50 bar H2, a reaction time of 5 h, and n-dodecane as solvent. These conditions were selected based on previous studies on model compounds investigating the influence of temperature and hydrogen pressure on HDO selectivity with the aim of enhancing the selectivity to naphthenes over aromatics.15,41 The reaction temperature (300°C) was chosen as a compromise that enables effective C–O bond cleavage while still promoting aromatic ring hydrogenation, an exothermic step that becomes suppressed at higher temperatures.15 The hydrogen pressure (50 bar H2) was selected to ensure sufficient hydrogen availability to favor ring hydrogenation and enhance cycloalkane formation.15 In total, four different catalysts were evaluated: Ru/C, Pd/C, Ni/SiO2, and phosphidated Ni/SiO2 (Ni2P/SiO2). Under the applied reaction conditions, all catalysts promoted the formation of naphthenic hydrocarbons with no detectable aromatics in the HDO products.

The HDO products were analyzed using GC-MS/FID (see section A.8 of the supplemental information for experimental details). Throughout this manuscript, the quantity of hydrocarbons is expressed as a carbon yield relative to the theoretical maximum (relative carbon yield [RCY]), as explained in section A.8 of the supplemental information. Noteworthy, the RCY allows us to compare the HDO performances of the different feedstocks in retaining their embedded carbon, while accounting for the inevitable carbon loss due to the demethoxylation (DMO) reactions, forming methane, occurring during HDO, as explained in detail in section A.8 of the supplemental information.39,41,43 In total, 30 hydrocarbons ranging from C6 to C18 were structurally identified (see Table S14 in the supplemental information for the complete list) and quantified. Their identification was facilitated by the availability of clear structural information on monomers and dimers, which enabled the back-tracing of C6–C18 hydrocarbons to the known potential precursors. By contrast, hydrocarbons with carbon numbers above C18 could not be structurally identified with certainty due to the lack of clear structural information on potential precursors (e.g., trimers, tetramers, and larger oligomers). Nevertheless, hydrocarbons in the C19–C27 range were included in the quantification, with their carbon numbers estimated based on their molecular ion masses obtained via MS. Since C19–C27 fall outside the jet range, their detailed structural elucidation is beyond the scope of this study. Overall, the identified and quantified cycloalkanes were categorized by their carbon number as monomer derived (C6–C11), dimer derived (C12–C18), and oligomer derived (C19–C27) (see Figure 3).

Overall, pronounced differences in product distribution and HDO efficiency were observed depending on the catalyst employed. The selectivity toward monomer-derived (C6–C11), dimer-derived (C12–C18), and oligomer-derived (C19–C27) hydrocarbons, as well as residual oxygenates, is reported in Figure 3 (left axis), while the total RCY is shown on the right axis. Detailed carbon-number-based hydrocarbon yields are provided in Table S15.

In general, Ni2P/SiO2 and unmodified Ni/SiO2 exhibited the highest RCY of C6–C27 hydrocarbons, reaching 71% and 69%, respectively. However, unmodified Ni/SiO2 showed a more pronounced and non-selective hydrocracking behavior compared to Ni2P/SiO2, as evidenced by its higher selectivity toward monomer-derived hydrocarbons and the concomitant decrease in dimer-derived products (Figure 3). This unselective hydrocracking activity was further confirmed by the formation of several light linear hydrocarbons originating from the undesired cracking of the n-dodecane solvent. Such non-selective solvent conversion complicated product analysis and mass-balance calculations, due to the generation of numerous hydrocracking products not derived from lignin. Moreover, Ru/C displayed an overall RCY of 57% with the highest selectivity toward monomer-derived hydrocarbons (C6–C11) among the tested catalysts (Figure 3), highlighting its strong hydrogenation capability. While this behavior confirms the effectiveness of Ru-based catalysts in converting high-MW lignin-derived species, the excessive cracking activity resulted in a very low selectivity toward dimer-derived hydrocarbons (C12–C18). Since these products are crucial for achieving a balanced hydrocarbon distribution suitable for SAF applications, Ru/C appears overly aggressive compared to both Ni/SiO2 and Ni2P/SiO2, leading to a less favorable product slate. In addition, Ru/C exhibited the highest yield of C8 and C7 mono-naphthenes (13% and 10%, respectively), while showing a lower yield of C9 mono-naphthenes (14%) compared to both Ni/SiO2 and Ni2P/SiO2 (22% and 24%, respectively). This shift toward lighter products indicates a pronounced contribution of reaction pathways leading to extensive carbon loss under the applied conditions. Finally, Pd/C showed poor overall HDO performance under the same conditions (Figure 3). The catalyst did not exhibit high selectivity toward either monomer- or dimer-derived hydrocarbons and was the only catalyst among those tested for which a significant fraction of oxygenated compounds remained in the product mixture (Figure 3), indicating incomplete deoxygenation. These results demonstrate the limited suitability of Pd/C for effective HDO of RLO under the conditions investigated.

Overall, among the catalysts evaluated, Ni2P/SiO2 proved to be the most suitable for the HDO of RLO under the investigated conditions. It delivered the highest overall RCY while maintaining a balanced distribution between monomer- and dimer-derived hydrocarbons. Importantly, phosphidation effectively mitigated the non-selective hydrocracking observed with unmodified Ni/SiO2, thereby suppressing undesired cracking pathways. These findings further rationalize the choice of Ni2P/SiO2 as a more selective catalyst for preserving SAF-relevant hydrocarbons while maintaining effective deoxygenation.

Nevertheless, the reusability of the Ni2P/SiO2 catalyst was evaluated by performing a second HDO reaction on whole RLO using the recovered catalyst. After reaction, the catalyst was separated by centrifugation, thoroughly washed with heptane, dried, and reduced as described in section A.4 of the supplemental information. While a decrease in overall hydrocarbon yield was observed compared to the fresh catalyst, the changes in product distribution were moderate. Notably, the used catalyst exhibited an increased selectivity toward oligomer-derived hydrocarbons (C19–C27), consistent with a partial loss of hydrogenation activity (Figure 3).

HDO of lignin oil and subfractions

The six fractions from H100 to E100, along with the entire RLO, were subjected to HDO at 300°C and 50 bar of hydrogen for 5 h over phosphidated Ni/SiO2, as described in section A.4 of the supplemental information. As previously anticipated, the identified and quantified cycloalkanes were categorized by their carbon number as: monomer derived (C6–C11), dimer derived (C12–C18), and oligomer derived (C19–C27). This categorization enabled us to further relate the HDO products to the components in RLO and its subfractions. A comprehensive discussion of the HDO mechanism explaining these categories will be provided in the following two sections. When examining the different RLO fractions during HDO, it was found that RCY consistently decreased from H100-HDO (81%) to E100-HDO (25%), as shown in Figure 4. Additionally, the RLO-HDO yielded a cumulative carbon yield of 71%, distributed as 44% of monomers-derived (C6–C11), 20% of dimers-derived (C12–C18), and 7% of oligomers-derived (C19–C27) hydrocarbons. Notably, the cumulative HDO yield from all six RLO-derived fractions, when normalized by their respective weight percentages relative to the original RLO, is fairly comparable to that of the yield from RLO-HDO. This confirms the reliability of the fractionation procedure and the consistency of the subsequent HDO treatment.

The observed progressive decrease in the RCY from H100-HDO to E100-HDO indicates that the earliest fractions—richer in monomers, dimers, and trimers (Figure S2)—retain a greater amount of carbon within the C6–C27 product range. This trend directly correlates with the MW distribution of the fractions, where lighter fractions exhibit higher RCY compared to those enriched in heavier species (Figure S7). This observation aligns with our previous study, which identified high MW as a key factor negatively impacting the HDO performance.43 More specifically, the poor performance of high-MW fractions as HDO feedstocks can be attributed to (1) the presence of large, unconverted molecules that may form coke or deposit heavy carbon on the catalyst due to steric and reactivity limitations; and (2) even when conversion does occur, the resulting hydrocarbons may exceed C27, falling outside the limit boiling point of detection—far beyond the SAF range. Additionally, the fractionation protocol follows an increasing polarity of the extractive solvent from H100 to E100. As a result, earlier fractions are expected to contain lower amounts of oxygenated EU (γ-OH and γ-O-Me) and oxygenated I-ULs (β-5 γ-OH, β-1 γ-OH, β-β 2x γ-OH, and β-β THF), as confirmed by 1H-13C HSQC analysis (see supplemental notes section B.2 of the supplemental information; Figures S3 and S4). In this context, fractions with higher content of oxygenated EU tend to retain less carbon during HDO, due to dehydrogenation and subsequent decarbonylation (DH/DCN) which leads to additional carbon loss, as discussed in our previous study.43 Extending this reasoning to oxygenated I-ULs present in dimers, trimers, and larger oligomers may further explain the lower RCY observed over the fractions enriched in these species.

In addition, to understand the overall deviation of the observed RCY from the theoretical maximum for the HDO products of the six fractions and the entire RLO, two aspects should be considered: (1) the RCY values reported in this study might represent a conservative estimation, as the paraffins potentially derived from the feedstocks have been excluded due to their indistinguishable overlap with solvent-derived species, as explained in detail in section A.8 of the supplemental information; (2) the theoretical maximum was calculated using a simplified lignin model (section A.8 of the supplemental information), which may not accurately reflect the structural diversity of lignin-derived molecules present in the RLO and its fractions—which can be subject to different HDO chemistry—resulting in an over-estimation of the achievable maximum.

From a macroscopic perspective, the six fractions contribute very differently to preserving the carbon embedded in the original backbone within the SAF range (C8–C18). The SAF-range RCY shows a pronounced decreasing trend from H100-HDO (74%) to E100-HDO (19.2%), with intermediate fractions exhibiting a gradual decline (Figure 4). The first fraction, H100—which represents the largest fraction by weight, accounting for 40 wt % of the initial RLO (Table S1)—retains most of the carbon into the SAF range (Figure 4). This makes it the major contributor to the final SAF product, as well as a key determinant of the overall composition of the final SAF blend. In addition, H80 and H60—which comprise 10.7 and 17 wt % of the initial RLO, respectively (Table S1)—also retain a significant portion of the initial carbon into the SAF range (Figure 4). By contrast, H40 and H20—which make up 15 and 8wt % of the original RLO, respectively (Table S1)—convert a substantial portion of their initial carbon into high-boiling-point hydrocarbons (C19–C27) outside of the SAF range (Figure 4), resulting in a decrease of the SAF-range RCY for H40-HDO and H20-HDO. Finally, E100-HDO shows the lowest SAF-range RCY, failing to preserve the initial carbon into a specific class of hydrocarbons, making E100 the lowest contributor to the final SAF blend.

The following two sections provide a molecular-level analysis of the different fractions to uncover the HDO pathways of lignin-derived monomers and dimers, the primary contributors to the SAF carbon range from lignin oil. This analysis reveals how each fraction influences the final SAF chemical composition by back-tracing the transformation of individual species.

Monomer-derived hydrocarbons

The C6–C11 naphthenes obtained from the HDO of RLO-derived fractions were attributed to monomeric origins based on carbon number and structural congruence with known lignin-derived monomers. Notably, the cumulative RCY of C6–C11 naphthenes exhibits a strong linear correlation with the cumulative monomeric carbon yield across the various fractions, as illustrated in Figure S9. Fractions enriched in monomers—such as H100 and H80—demonstrated the highest RCYs in the C6–C11 range, whereas heavier fractions such as H20 and E100 yielded significantly lower quantities (Figures 5A and 5B). This clear trend underscores that the formation of C6–C11 naphthenes is predominantly driven by the HDO transformation of monomeric species within each fraction.

Interestingly, fractions such as H40-, H20-, and E100-HDO also produced measurable quantities of C6–C11 naphthenes despite the near absence of monomers in their corresponding feedstocks (Figures 5A and 5B). This observation indicates that the Ni phosphide catalyst not only preserves monomer structures but also facilitates the cleavage of inter-unit C–C bonds via hydrogenolysis, enabling the generation of mono-cyclic naphthenes from dimeric and oligomeric precursors. For example, in the H100 fraction, the carbon yield of monomers (Figure 5A) closely aligns with the RCY of mono-naphthenes post HDO (Figure 5B), demonstrating the structural integrity of monomeric skeletons under HDO conditions. Conversely, in fractions with a higher prevalence of oligomeric species—such as H80 through E100 (Figure 5A)—RCY of mono-naphthenes consistently surpasses the carbon yield attributable to monomers (Figure 5B), substantiating the significant contribution of dimers, trimers, and higher oligomers to the formation of mono-naphthenes during HDO.

In terms of molecular structures, most products are mono-naphthenes, i.e., constituted by single C5 or C6 naphthenic ring (entry 1–17 of Table S14). As previously reported, these moieties are known to result from HDO pathways of lignin model compounds.49,51,52,82,83 Consequently, each major mono-naphthene will be herein correlated to its parent lignin monomer in the respective fraction with a proposed reaction pattern. Moreover, the distribution of these mono-naphthenes over the RLO-HDO subfraction will be discussed. To accomplish this, each of the potential parent RLO monomers present across the fractions and in the RLO are classified based on their carbon backbone, excluding the methoxy carbon, which is inevitably removed forming methane through DMO.

Notably, H100-HDO shows the highest RCY of C9 naphthenes (54.0%), which drastically decreases over the fractions (Figure 5B). Among C9, propyl cyclohexane is the most abundant hydrocarbon, with its RCY changing across the fractions as follows: H100-HDO (53.4%) > H80-HDO (8.3%) > H60-HDO (4.7%) > H40-HDO (2.8%) > H20-HDO (2.3%) > E100-HDO (2.0%), as indicated in Figure S10. From a mechanistic perspective, the formation of propyl cyclohexane is attributed to HDO of parent 4-propyl- and propenyl-substituted monomers. These conversions are in good agreement with the HDO studies conducted using propyl- and propenyl-substituted monomer model compounds.16,49,52 Herein, the process involves removal of the methoxy group via DMO, the hydrogenation (HYD) of the aromatic ring, and the elimination of the phenolic hydroxyl group through direct deoxygenation (DDO).84,85 Together, these transformations enable preserving the C9 carbon backbone (Figure 5C). In this context, the highest RCY yield of propyl cyclohexane in H100-HDO is related to the highest wt % of propyl- and propenyl-substituted monomers in that fraction (Figure S6).

Unlike C9, C8 RCY shows a peaking behavior, being the highest in H80-HDO (15.0%) and H60-HDO (9.9%), as shown in Figure 5B. Notably, ethyl cyclohexane stands out as the most abundant C8 among the HDO products, as shown in Figure S10. In this case, ethyl cyclohexane can be generated through the conversion of both 4-ethyl- and 4-propanol-substituted parent monomers as shown in Figure 5C. For ethyl-substituted monomers, the carbon backbone is preserved, like the C9 previously discussed (Figure 5C). By contrast, the conversion of 4-propanol-substituted monomers follows a different mechanism due to the integration of dehydrogenation and subsequent decarbonylation (DHDC) during HDO.43,46,47 This reaction—herein denoted as HDO-DHDC—lead to loss of a single carbon atom from the initial backbone, yielding C8 naphthenes from the parent C9 monomer (Figure 5C), consistent with previous studies.43,46,47

Furthermore, among the C6–C11 mono-naphthenes, methyl cyclohexane (C7) and cyclohexane (C6) were the most abundant species within their respective carbon-number ranges; however, their contributions were substantially lower than those of the dominant C8 and C9 mono-naphthenes. Across the fractions, both compounds were present at low relative levels (typically around 1%–1.3%) with only modest variations between samples (Figure S10). The HDO formation of these lighter naphthenes follows the same multistep pathway involving DMO, HYD, and DDO as described for higher mono-naphthenes such as propyl- and ethyl cyclohexane (Figure 5C). In addition to the mono-naphthenes discussed above, a series of additional C6–C11 hydrocarbons, grouped as others, was identified (Figure S10; Table S14, entry 1–17). The RCY of these species varies across the fractions, with higher contributions observed for the lighter fractions (e.g., H100-HDO and H80-HDO) and progressively lower contributions for heavier fractions, indicating a decreasing formation of these secondary products with increasing fraction heaviness.

These “others” hydrocarbons include (1) C6–C9 substituted cyclopentane arising from skeletal isomerization of the most abundant naphthenes (e.g., C8-propyl-cyclopentane [entry 8, Table S14] from C8-ethyl-cyclohexane); (2) alkylated C6–C9 mono-naphthenes, typically involving methylation reaction (e.g., C10-1-methyl-2-propyl-cyclohexane from C9-propyl-cyclohexane); (3) condensation products yielding bi-naphthenes (e.g., C11-2-methyl-decahydronaphthalene). Overall, the first transformation preserves the carbon backbone, while the second and third cases result in an increase in carbon number. A comprehensive scheme detailing some of the proposed additional pathways of conversion toward others monomer-derived hydrocarbons is reported in Scheme 1.

Skeletal isomerization of cycloalkanes to substituted cyclopentanes has been reported as a secondary reaction during HDO of lignin-derived phenolic model compounds and is generally associated with acid-catalyzed transformations at elevated temperatures.44,51,52,85,86 In nickel phosphide systems, such transformations may be associated with the bifunctional character of the catalyst under the applied HDO conditions.87 Moreover, methylation of lignin-derived hydrocarbons has been reported during HDO of methoxy-phenol model compounds.86,88,89 In particular, methoxy-removal reactions have been proposed to generate methyl-containing intermediates that may participate in subsequent alkylation reactions under elevated-temperature HDO conditions.86 This pathway can lead to the formation of alkylated mono-naphthenes such as C10-1-methyl-2-propyl-cyclohexane (Scheme 1). As alkylation reactions are generally favored by acid functionality, the limited acidity of Ni2P/SiO2 rationalizes the minor abundance of these methylated products, consistent with the bifunctional yet moderately acidic nature of the employed catalyst.86,89 Interestingly, an enhanced methylation of naphthenic compounds obtained during HDO would be highly beneficial to the atom efficiency of the whole process by preventing carbon loss. Finally, condensed polycyclic hydrocarbons, such as C11-2-methyl-decahydronaphthalene (Scheme 1), have been reported as side products during lignin HDO.41,90 In general, their formation is associated with condensation reactions between lignin-derived intermediates prior to complete HDO.91 Such processes are typically promoted under acidic conditions and in environments where reactive phenolic intermediates persist.15,91,92 In one-pot HDO systems operating under strongly hydrogenating conditions, rapid stabilization of intermediates limits their availability for secondary condensation pathways. In the present case, the combination of a highly hydrogenating environment and the moderate acidity of Ni2P/SiO2 rationalizes the formation of fused polycyclic hydrocarbons only in trace amounts.

Overall, the conversion of lignin-derived 4-substituted guaiacol monomers plays a pivotal role in shaping the final composition of the RLO-derived SAF blend. The high abundance of monomers in the parent RLO and its derived fractions (Figure 1) therefore leads to a final SAF blend enriched in the mono-naphthenes that has shown promising potential for aviation applications, as reported in previous studies.39,91,93,94 The predominance of propyl-substituted monomers across the fractions (especially in H100) enables a high RCY of C9 mono-naphthenes—particularly propyl cyclohexane—as previously discussed. Since H100 represents the largest fraction by weight (Table S12), the resulting RLO-derived SAF blend is predominantly composed of propyl cyclohexane. In the context of SAF production, propyl cyclohexane showed favorable physicochemical properties—namely, high specific energy (>42.8 MJ/kg),95,96 energy density (>33.7 MJ/L),3,93 and boiling points that fall well within the aviation turbine fuel range (125°C–290°C)95,97—thus ensuring compatibility with established jet fuel specifications.3,8,96 By contrast, C8 mono-naphthenes are generated in lower amounts, in line with the relatively lower abundance of 4-propanol-substituted monomers, the precursors to compounds such as ethyl cyclohexane. Hence, the lower amount of C8 mono-naphthenes compared to C9 mono-naphthenes in the HDO product fractions is in line with the hydrocarbon profile of conventional aviation fuel, where the content of C8 generally is lower than that of C9.3,8 Furthermore, the monomer composition (Figure S6) inherently limits the formation of C6 and C7 naphthenes—undesirable for SAF applications due to their too-low boiling point and energy densities—making their absence actually beneficial.3 In addition, the small amounts of C10–C11 naphthenes, formed via alkylation or condensation pathways, were also detected. While their low concentration indicates they play only a minor role in determining the final SAF-blend composition, these compounds do fall within the desirable carbon-number window for SAF.

Dimer-derived hydrocarbons

Analogous to monomers, the naphthenes with carbon numbers ranging between C12 and C18 have been associated primarily with the HDO of lignin dimers. These molecules structurally resemble the lignin-derived dimers (Tables S5–S13) due to their bi-naphthenic nature (Table S14, entry 18–30) and original number of interlinkage carbons. As previously described, the parent lignin dimers have been classified and categorized based on their carbon backbone, which ranges from C12 to C18 (see Figure 6A). Interestingly, when compared with the produced naphthenes along the six fractions the RCY of C12 to C18 bi-naphthenes aligns well with the carbon content of the dimers in the parent fractions, as shown in Figures 6A and 6B. This correlation is particularly strong for the initials fraction (i.e., H100-H60 HDO). By contrast, the latter fractions, from H40-HDO to E100-HDO, presented a relatively high RCY of C12–C18, despite their parent fractions containing negligible amount of dimers (Figures 6A and 5B). These results can be attributed to the I-ULs’ cleavage of trimers, tetramers, and larger oligomers during HDO, which leads to the formation of C12–C18 bi-naphthenes. This chemistry is similar to what was previously observed with the C6–C11 mono-naphthenes found in the same fractions.

Overall, the fractions containing the highest concentrations of dimers—namely H60 and H80—also demonstrate the greatest RCYs of C12–C18 hydrocarbons. This strong correspondence suggests that these hydrocarbon products predominantly originate from the transformation of lignin-derived dimeric precursors. To develop a mechanistic, molecular-level understanding of the HDO conversion pathways for these parent dimers, the ensuing discussion will systematically examine the HDO behavior of the principal dimer species. This analysis will be organized according to their carbon backbones (C14–C18) and the specific types of (original) I-ULs they contain, which play critical roles in determining reactivity and product distribution (mostly β-1, β-5, 5-5, and β-β).

Among the parent lignin-derived dimers, β-1 dimers present a carbon backbone ranging from C14 to or C15, depending on the substitution on the I-UL (β′ substituent) (see Figure 6C). The structure of these dimers closely resembles the bi-naphthene products, which also possess a carbon backbone ranging from C14 to C15 (entry 22–23, Table S14). Accordingly, these types of dimers are the most abundant precursor of C14–C15 bi-naphthenes. Notably, β-1-linked dimers constitute a relatively small class that varies primarily based on the type of substituents at the β position of the I-UL. Consequently, the mechanism of HDO within this class of dimers depends on the variation in the I-UL. For instance, β-1 dimers with C14–C15 carbon backbone and no oxygenated I-UL undergo HDO by directly converting into C14 and C15 bi-naphthenes, as shown in Figure 6C. Such an HDO mechanism is mostly followed in fraction H80, which is rich in β-1 dimers with C14 backbone and devoid of oxygenated I-UL (Figure 6A; Table S11). In this case, H80-HDO exhibited the second highest RCY of C14 bi-naphthenes (4%).

Conversely, β-1 dimers with oxygenated substitution at the β position of the I-UL undergo HDO with dehydration and decarbonylation (HDO-DHDC) reaction on the I-UL. This mechanism results in the loss of one carbon from their backbone, yielding C14 bi-naphthenes from a C15 parent dimer. This is evident in H60-HDO, which exhibits the highest C14 RCY (5.4%), as shown in Figure 6B. In this context, the parent fraction H60 contains the highest content of β-1 dimers with C15 carbon backbone and oxygenated I-UL (Figure S11A), leading to HDO-DHDC conversion toward C14 bi-naphthenes (Figure S11B). This finding is consistent with previously described conversion mechanism for monomers with oxygenated EU and is thus also applicable to dimers with oxygenated I-ULs.

Overall, the β-1 I-UL is a two-carbon linkage (Figure 6C)—referring to the minimum number of carbon atoms in the I-UL excluding any substituent—that is retained during the HDO in the resulting bi-naphthenes.

Additionally, β-5, β-β, and 5-5 dimers present a carbon backbone ranging from C16 to C18 (Figure 6), making these dimers the principal precursors to C16–C18 bi-naphthenes, following a similar rationale to that applied for β-1 dimers. Among the parent lignin dimers, the β-5 dimers are the most abundant in both RLO and in its subfractions (see Figure 2). Specifically, the β-5 dimers possess a relatively wide carbon backbone that varies between C16 and C18 depending by the different substituents on the β and 1 position (see Tables S5–S7 in supplemental information). Similarly, 5-5 and β-5 I-UL parent dimers fall in the same C16–C18 carbon backbone, depending on their 1-1 and β-β substituents, respectively. Notably, in contrast to β-1 linked dimers, β-5 and 5-5 dimers may have various EU chains substituted at position 1 on the aromatic ring. Consequently, the mechanism of conversion within this class of dimers depends on (1) both the β substituent on the I-UL, as well as the type of EU for β-5, and (2) the type of EU for 5-5 dimers.

Consequently, β-5 dimers with carbon backbone of C18—without oxygenated I-UL as well as EU—and 5-5 dimers with C18 carbon backbone—without oxygenated EU—can be directly transformed into C18 bi-naphthenes while preserving the carbon backbone during HDO, as shown in Figure 6C. These types of dimers are the largest source of C18 bi-naphthenes among the fractions from H100-HDO to E100-HDO. By contrast, β-5 dimers with carbon backbone of C18 that contain only oxygenated I-UL or EU are subject to HDO-DHDC, resulting in a loss of one carbon compared to the parent dimer. In particular, H60-HDO shows the highest RCY of such C17 bi-naphthene products (17%), attributed to the highest concentration of this type of β-5 dimers (see Figure 2; Tables S5–S7). Additionally, β-5 dimers with carbon backbone of C18—with both oxygenated I-UL as well as EU—are subject to HDO-DHDC chemistry, yielding C16 bi-naphthenes, due to double loss of carbon atom (Figure 6C). Similarly, 5-5 dimers—which can accommodate double EU on both the phenolics in the dimer structures—exhibit a comparable behavior depending on the type of EU, as shown in Figure 6C. This explains how β-5 and 5-5 dimers, primarily with carbon backbone of mostly C18, are the biggest precursors to C16–C18 bi-naphthenes with the highest RCY of C17 bi-naphthenes (Figure 6B). A more detailed scheme for the proposed conversion pathways of the most abundant β-5 and 5-5 dimers identified across the fractions is provided in Scheme 2. Similarly to β-1, the β-5 I-UL also qualifies as a two-carbon linkage (Figure 6C), with the two carbon atoms from the I-UL retained in the resulting naphthene structures. By contrast, the 5-5 linkage is a zero-carbon linkage (Figure 6C), since the connection between the two units does not contribute any carbon atoms to the final hydrocarbon backbone.

Finally, β-β linked dimers present a carbon backbone of C18 that may feature oxygenated substituents on the I-UL (β-β 2x γ-OH), primarily resulting in the formation of C16 bi-naphthenes through the double-carbon loss due to HDO-DHDC. The β-β I-UL is a four-carbon linkage (Figure 6C), with all the four carbon atoms within the I-UL preserved in the final naphthene structure.

Nevertheless, the RCY of C12–C13 bi-naphthenes remains low across all fractions, with only minor variations observed between samples (Figure 6B). Overall, these species contribute marginally to the total product slate, with RCY values generally below 1%–1.5%. This minor subset of hydrocarbons is primarily formed through carbon-carbon cracking reactions occurring at the EUs of prevalent bi-naphthenes, particularly those derived from 5-5 linked dimers, as illustrated in Scheme 2.

The conversion of lignin-derived dimers significantly contributes to the final hydrocarbon profile of the RLO-derived SAF blend. Guaiacol dimers represent the second most abundant molecular class after the monomers (Figure 1) and play a key role in determining the composition of the bi-naphthenes present in the final fuel composition. Among the resulting products, C14–C18 bi-naphthenes are the most abundant, with C17 emerging as the most dominant component. This trend is driven by the prevalence of β-5 dimers across the fractions (Figure 2), which serve—as discussed above—as direct precursors to C17 hydrocarbons. Other dimer types, such as β-1, also contribute notably, yielding primarily C14 and C15 bi-naphthenes. Even though many lignin-derived dimers share a common C18 backbone, the final yield of the corresponding C18 hydrocarbons is comparatively low, and this is due to carbon loss that occurs during HDO via the chemical pathway referred to as HDO-DHC, in the presence of the Ni phosphide catalyst. In total, H80, H60, and H40 account for 10.7, 17, and 15 wt % of the initial RLO, respectively (Table S1). These fractions have the highest content of dimers (Figure 2), making them the principal contributors to C14–C17 bi-naphthenes in the final SAF product. However, H40 delivers the highest RCY of high-boiling-point naphthenes (C19–C27) outside the SAF range, yet its overall RCY is lower compared to H100, H80, and H60. This is due to its enrichment in high-MW lignin fragments. Despite these drawbacks, given its significant wt % relative to the initial feedstock and its contribution to formation of C14–C17 bi-naphthenes, H40 can still be considered as an important contributor to high-quality SAF blend.

Given the composition of the six fractions (Figure 1) and their weight percentages relative to the initial oil (Table S1), it is evident that the quantity of bi-naphthenes is lower compared to mono-naphthenes in the final SAF blend. Nevertheless, bi-naphthenes constitute the second major naphthenic class and fall well within the carbon-number range typical of jet fuels.3,8 This composition is expected to support an appropriate boiling range and contribute to the overall volatility and energy density of the fuel.14,94 In contrast to some earlier studies where an excessive presence of dicyclic compounds led to elevated boiling points and limited drop-in potential, the more balanced distribution observed here aligns well with reported SAF-relevant fuel properties.14

Conclusions and outlook

In conclusion, the solvent-driven fractionation of RCF-derived RLO enabled a distinct molecular delineation of its constituent classes and illuminated the structural determinants that govern HDO behavior. This integrated, two-tiered investigation—spanning both the RCF and HDO stages—proved critical for elucidating how the chemical composition and physicochemical attributes of each fraction dictate the formation of specific naphthenic hydrocarbons, particularly the mono- and bi-cyclic species that dominate the HDO product spectrum. The results underscore that the intrinsic molecular architecture of the feedstock exerts a direct influence on the hydrocarbon distribution, thereby shaping the performance and suitability of the resulting blend for SAF applications. Altogether, this comprehensive approach not only deepens our mechanistic insight into the reactivity of lignin-derived molecules but also establishes a strategic framework for tailoring SAF-range fuel precursors from renewable lignocellulose biomass. The HDO of fractions H100, H80, H60, and H40 resulted predominantly in the formation of C8–C18 hydrocarbons, a molecular range highly desirable for SAF applications. Notably, the RCY within the SAF-relevant C8–C18 window follows a decreasing trend: H100-HDO (74%) > H80-HDO (55.4%) > H60-HDO (52%) > H40-HDO (35.4%).

Compositional analysis revealed that the monomer-rich H100 fraction preferentially yields C8–C11 mono-naphthenes, with C9-propyl-cyclohexane emerging as the predominant product, accounting for 54% RCY—making it the most abundant mono-naphthene observed across all fractions. The second most prevalent class of mono-naphthenes is represented by C8 species, with H80 generating the highest RCY of C8-ethyl-cyclohexane (14%), the second most abundant mono-naphthene overall. By contrast, the dimer-enriched fractions—H80, H60, and H40—tend to favor the generation of C12–C18 bi-naphthenes. Among these, H60 displayed the highest RCY of C17 bi-naphthenes (17%), which also emerged as the most dominant bi-naphthenic species across the dataset.

Collectively, these findings underscore the synergistic role of monomeric and dimeric constituents in shaping the hydrocarbon distribution within the SAF-compatible range. The molecular composition of each fraction directly steers the selectivity toward either mono- or bi-naphthenic products, offering valuable insights for tuning feedstock-processing strategies aimed at maximizing SAF yields.

Unlike H100, H80, H60, and H40, the fraction H20 is not well suited for high-quality SAF production due to its high contribution to high-boiling point C19–C27 hydrocarbons and the lower carbon efficiency, both of which are related to its high concentration of high-MW molecules. Similarly, the E100 fraction shows the lowest RCY and does not significantly contribute to any desirable hydrocarbon class. Overall, these two heavy fractions contribute to approximately 12.3 wt % of the entire RLO—i.e., H20 (8 wt %) and E100 (4.3 wt %). The H20 and E100 fractions exhibit high weight-average MWs of 1,430 and 2,728, respectively, and are primarily composed of species larger than trimers, as shown by GPC analysis. In addition, GC×GC analysis confirms that the content of monomers and dimers in these fractions is negligible, while 1H-13C HSQC NMR further reveals that these fractions contain the highest abundance of inter-unit linkages among all samples—predominantly highly polar oxygenated inter-unit linkages such as β-β 2x γ-OH and β-5 γ-OH. These observations explain their limited carbon efficiency and tendency to yield products unsuitable for SAF applications during HDO. A better understanding—possibly accessible through advanced analytical techniques—could enhance our comprehension of their properties and guide their application for SAF purposes.

However, selectively removing these heavy fractions also opens avenues for alternative value-added applications more aligned with their known structural features. In fact, lignin-derived oligomers have been already explored for applications to materials such as replacement of p-nonylphenol in printing ink,67 of bisphenol A in thermosets,77 or for bio-based polyurethane precursors.78,98,99 From a biorefinery perspective, valorizing these heavy fractions as well may enhance the overall carbon efficiency and economic viability of the entire process. Consequently, fractionation may evolve into a multifunctional platform that is tunable for selective production of SAF precursors and diversified bioproduct development.

This study also promotes fractionation of RLO not merely as an analytical technique but as a strategic lever to align the product distribution with the SAF-relevant hydrocarbon profile. By selectively isolating and processing the most reactive and compositionally advantageous fractions, the yield of C8–C18 naphthenes can be significantly enhanced—highlighting the promise of this approach as an efficient and scalable pathway for SAF production. As an example, this approach would reduce the formation of high-MW hydrocarbons (>C17), which are known for negatively impacting the cold-flow properties limiting the blending ratio with conventional aviation fuel or other SAFs.

Moreover, this lab-scale proof of concept has the potential to pave the way toward possible industrial upscaling of the solvent-based fractionation. To this end, a thorough techno-economic study will be essential to assess its viability. Alternatively, industrially established separation methods—such as distillation of lignin-derived intermediates—could be developed, guided by the structural and compositional criteria identified in this study that are favorable for SAF synthesis. Additionally, the findings of this manuscript reveal that distinct classes of lignin-derived monomers and dimers undergo HDO to yield well-defined hydrocarbon structures. This molecular-level correlation can guide future strategies in biomass selection, design, and feedstock engineering—such as lignin modification or the use of engineered wood—to tailor the abundance of specific intermediates, thereby enabling the targeted production of specific subclasses of hydrocarbons.

In addition, the selective conversion of monomer- or dimer-rich fractions opens opportunities for future research aimed at fine-tuning the carbon distribution of the final product. For instance, controlled cracking of high-MW species (>C27) and enhancing in situ (trans)alkylation could improve the overall SAF yield with minimal carbon loss. In particular, in situ reactions that can upgrade mono-naphthenes to longer-chain molecules could help meet SAF carbon requirements as well in an overall atom-efficient approach. These directions highlight the importance of integrating molecular-level insights with process development and economic considerations to advance lignin valorization for SAF applications.

Nevertheless, including separation techniques in the framework of SAF production from lignin oil could allow the development of a superior RCF-to-SAF biorefinery scheme for the production of high-quality naphthenes for SAF blends.

text:
insights.ias

2h

Take flight toward a greener future! ✈️🌱

The Indian government has just made a major move in the aviation sector by officially bringing Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)-blended fuel under its regulatory umbrella. This isn't just a technical update; it’s a massive step toward decarbonizing our skies! 🌍✨

🔍 What exactly is SAF?

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is a "drop-in" solution. This means it can be blended with traditional Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) and used in existing aircraft engines without needing any expensive modifications. 🛠️🚫

🧪 Composition & Nature

Chemical Twin: It consists of specially processed hydrocarbons that are chemically similar to petroleum-based ATF.

Eco-Friendly Feedstocks: Derived from renewable sources like crops, biogenic residues, and various waste materials. ♻️

Seamless Compatibility: Fully compatible with current fueling systems and infrastructure.

⚖️ Governance & New Regulations

The government has amended the ATF (Regulation of Marketing) Order, 2001 (ATF Control Order) to include these blends. 📄✅

IS 1571: Standard for petroleum ATF and co-processed SAF.

IS 17081: The specific standard for SAF blended with traditional ATF.

🌏 Why this matters globally

This move aligns India with the ICAO’s CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation). Starting in 2027, international flights must offset emissions—and using SAF is a key way to do that! 📉

💡 The Big Impact

By expanding the definition of ATF to include SAF co-processed in refineries, India is helping domestic carriers meet international standards, reducing the financial burden of buying carbon credits, and—most importantly—slashing our carbon footprint. 🌬️💚

The future of flying is sustainable, and India is leading the way! 🇮🇳✈️

text:
Fry cooks at the nearly 14,000 McDonald's restaurants across the United States go through a lot of oil. Employees say most restaurants change their fry oil about once a week. When that oil is no longer fit for the fryer, it does not have to go to waste, and at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, it has not been going to waste since 2019.

In partnership with Finnish sustainable fuel producer Neste, DFW Airport collects used cooking oil from 5 McDonald's locations and other airport restaurants, approximately 32,000 pounds of it every month — and converts it into sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF. The process starts simply: food particles from french fries and McNuggets are filtered out, the oil is heated, and hydrogen is added. The refinery then breaks down the oil's hydrocarbon molecules and rebuilds them to mimic the chemical structure of conventional jet fuel. The end result is a fuel that can be blended with traditional petroleum jet fuel and used in aircraft engines with no modification required. According to Neste, 1 gallon of recycled cooking oil produces about three-quarters of a gallon of SAF.

The process works because vegetable oils and jet fuel are not as chemically different as they might seem. Both are built around hydrocarbon molecules. "If you look at any oil, they all have these building molecules, hydrocarbons," said Pratik Chandhoke, sustainable aviation fuel technical services manager at Neste US. "We can take those atoms and then do some processing magic in our refineries and we actually mimic the chemistry of a jet fuel." The result is the same jet fuel that powers aircraft across the country, it just started in a fryer.

text:
Mexico ranked 17th globally in airport-related CO₂ emissions in 2023, generating 15.5 million tons, equivalent to 2% of total sector emissions, according to ODI Global. The country is part of a group of 20 nations that account for 78% of global airport emissions, based on data from 1,300 airports tracked worldwide, which collectively produced 1.022 billion tons of CO₂ during the year.

The ranking reflects the scale of aviation activity and the concentration of emissions in key markets. The United States led with 259.4 million tons, or 25% of the total, followed by China with 138.2 million tons, or 13%. Other countries in the top 20 include the United Kingdom, Japan, the United Arab Emirates, Germany, and India.

“The aviation sector remains a major contributor to climate change and air pollution. Emissions from air travel continue on an upward trend and show limited signs of reduction, due to the sector’s heavy reliance on sustainable aviation fuels and weak mitigation strategies,” ODI Global said in its study.

At the airport level, Dubai International recorded the highest emissions at 23.2 million tons of CO₂ in 2023, followed by London Heathrow with 21 million tons and Los Angeles International Airport with 18.8 million. Seoul Incheon and John F. Kennedy Airport each generated 16.8 million tons. At the city level, London ranked first with 29.2 million tons across six airports, followed by New York with 28.5 million and Dubai with 24.8 million.

In Latin America and the Caribbean, emissions are concentrated in a limited number of hubs. São Paulo/Guarulhos led the region with 6.8 million tons of CO₂ and 127,817 flights, followed by Mexico City with 4.9 million tons and 173,001 flights. Bogota El Dorado reported 3.6 million tons, while Cancún and Santiago Arturo Merino Benítez recorded 3.5 million and 3.2 million tons, respectively. Guadalajara ranked 10th with 1.5 million tons and 68,366 flights.

The data indicate that emissions are closely linked to traffic volumes and airport operations, including ground activity and infrastructure energy use. Mexico’s inclusion in the top 20 highlights the role of its airport system within the global aviation network.

At the same time, the sector faces constraints in reducing emissions. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), a central component of decarbonization strategies, is expected to reach only 0.7% of global demand by 2030. Costs remain three to five times higher than conventional jet fuel, limiting adoption and slowing investment in production capacity.

In response, Mexico’s federal government is advancing coordination efforts to integrate SAF into its aviation system. The Ministry of Infrastructure, Communications and Transportation (SICT), in coordination with Aeropuertos y Servicios Auxiliares (ASA), the Federal Civil Aviation Agency, and the Ministry of Energy (SE), will hold a technical forum to address policy, certification, financing, and production.

Global supply constraints remain a challenge. Energy companies have scaled back refinery projects due to limited demand visibility and uncertain returns, slowing supply expansion and reinforcing concerns among airlines about meeting regulatory targets.

Operational pressures are also affecting the sector. The International Air Transport Association said aircraft delivery delays added more than US$11 billion in costs in 2025, with about two-thirds linked to fuel consumption and maintenance. Airlines are operating aircraft that are, on average, two years older than historical norms.

“Unfortunately, we see that this disruption will continue for some time,” said Director General Willie Walsh. He added that older aircraft “consume more fuel and require more frequent maintenance,” increasing both costs and emissions.

The industry remains aligned with the International Civil Aviation Organization’s target of net-zero emissions by 2050, but cost pressures are intensifying. Willie Walsh warned airlines could face about US$60 billion in additional costs through 2035 under current carbon pricing. At the same time, a fuel crisis linked to tensions between Iran and the United States is shifting the conversation toward accelerating SAF implementation.

text:
Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOCL) has approved a joint venture with M11 Energy Transition Pvt. Ltd. for setting up a Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) project at Paradip, Odisha.

The proposed project will be developed at an estimated cost of ₹1,063.60 crore, with a variation margin of ±30%, according to the company’s regulatory filing dated 18 May 2026.

50:50 Venture Structure

The proposed entity will be formed as a 50:50 joint venture between Indian Oil and M11 Energy Transition. The project is subject to approvals from NITI Aayog and the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM).

The facility will manufacture 100 KTPA (kilo tonnes per annum) of HEFA-based Sustainable Aviation Fuel. HEFA, or Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids, is a technology used to produce aviation fuel from renewable feedstocks such as used cooking oil and vegetable oils.

Paradip Chosen for New Fuel Project

The project will come up at Paradip, where Indian Oil already operates a refinery and petrochemical complex. The location is considered important due to existing refining infrastructure and port connectivity.

The proposed SAF unit is to expand into lower-emission fuel segments alongside conventional refining operations.

Aviation Sector Looking at Cleaner Fuels

Demand for Sustainable Aviation Fuel has been increasing globally as airlines and fuel producers prepare for tighter emission reduction targets.

SAF is being explored as an alternative to conventional aviation turbine fuel due to its lower lifecycle carbon emissions.

India has also been examining the use of alternative fuels in aviation as part of energy transition and decarbonisation plans.

As of May 19, 2026, 12:14 pm, Indian Oil Corporation Ltd share price was trading at ₹135.80, a 3.03% increase from the previous closing price.

Indian Oil and M11 Energy Transition plan to develop the SAF project through a 50:50 joint venture structure at Paradip. The proposal remains subject to approvals from NITI Aayog and DIPAM.

text:
Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund is unlikely to meet its 2030 decarbonisation targets, its chief executive said, citing challenges in lowering the emissions of its aviation and energy-related holdings.

“Under current conditions — and given our portfolio exposure to hard-to-abate sectors — we are unlikely to meet our interim 2030 target to halve net portfolio emissions from 2010 levels,” said Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara, chief executive officer of Temasek Holdings.

Speaking at the opening dinner of the organisation’s annual Ecosperity conference on Monday, Sandrasegara clarified that Temsek has not retreated from its net zero pathway, which it aims to achieve by 2050.

“What we committed to achieving come 2030 still serves as an important directional marker, befitting of our ambition and we will continue to press forward on every available lever, but our pace must reflect today’s realities,” he said.

These “realities” include Temasek’s exposure to the aviation and power generation sectors, which are both lagging on decarbonisation.

In aviation, where the fund has been engaging in “real operational decarbonisation, and not simply offsets,” sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) still accounts for less than 1 per cent of global supply, Sandrasegara pointed out.

Singapore Airlines, in which Temasek owns a majority stake, said in a results briefing last week that it would be adding more flights to its global routes as other carriers pare down due to higher fuel prices triggered by the war in the Middle East.

“As a shareholder, we are, of course, pleased with this, but on the other hand, with our sustainability cap on, we lament the increase in the emissions arising from this,” said Sandrasegara.

“But if SIA does not do well, it will be debilitated from doing the right thing in terms of fleet renewal and SAF adoption,” he added.

Temasek’s energy investments have also contributed to the derailment of its near-term decarbonisation goals. Last December, Temasek-backed Sembcorp Industries announced the acquisition of Australia’s Alinta Energy, which holds a 10.4-gigawatt (GW) pipeline of renewable energy projects but also has no set date to power down a 1.2GW coal-fired power plant.

Sandrasegara acknowledged that Alinta’s coal plant supplies some 20 per cent of the state of Victoria’s electricity demand, but also emphasised the group’s “clear pathway towards a cleaner energy mix over time.”

“The reality is that the world cannot transition overnight,” said Sandrasegara. “A credible transition is not simply about shutting assets down quickly — it is about replacing them responsibly, while preserving energy security, affordability, and grid reliability along the way.”

He pointed out that Temasek’s portfolio emissions have declined by about 30 per cent since 2019, when it first set its climate targets. In 2024, the group recorded its first reduction in portfolio emissions — driven at the time by Sembcorp’s divestment of its Indian coal power business, a move that drew criticism in the way it accounted for emissions.

Today, however, volatile global markets and higher financing costs have affected the cost of capital and slowed long-term investments, said Sandrasegara, forcing investors confront “a collision between long-term ambition and near-term constraints”.

“Therefore, the transition will be far more uneven, contested and non-linear than previously anticipated,” he added.

text:
Source: CSTA via Brazil Energy

From CGN Brazil: In partnership with the Government of Piauí, we are advancing the structuring of an innovative initiative for the development of concentrated solar power (CSP) technology with thermal storage — still unprecedented in Brazil.

The agreement, signed with the Piauí Institute of Technology, provides for technical, economic and regulatory feasibility studies for the implementation of a first tower CSP project of approximately 100 MW in the state. The proposal aims to expand the supply of dispatchable renewable energy, helping to overcome challenges such as the intermittency of solar sources and grid evacuation constraints.

[Ed note: China’s SOEs have experience building infrastructure in Brazil. State Grid Corporation of China owns a large slice of Brazil’s electricity transmission network, acquired through a series of purchases from the 2010s onward. Chinese companies have built numerous wind and (PV) solar farms, despite a rocky relationship with the previous Bolsonaro government. CGN’s existing 506MW of solar (PV) and wind in Piauí suggests they know the local regulatory, grid and permitting environment.]

According to CGN Brasil president Mingzhu Li:

“The project represents an important step towards expanding the reliability of renewable energy in Brazil, combining technological innovation and regional development.

CSP technology with thermal storage stands out for enabling power generation even in the absence of sunlight, offering greater stability to the electricity system. With our consolidated experience with this technology in international projects, we reinforce its potential application in the Brazilian market.

The project will initially involve technical cooperation activities at the national level, including exchanges between Brazilian professionals and technical visits to operational plants in China.

As part of the technology development and talent formation strategy, a call will be launched to select students, master’s and doctoral candidates from universities across Brazil, who will contribute analyses and solutions to the project.

Piauí Governor Rafael Fonteles: “Piauí has sought to position itself as a hub of innovation in renewable energy. This partnership helps attract investment, generate knowledge and strengthen regional development.”

The RISE PA grant program is a $396 million statewide industrial decarbonization initiative funded through the U.S. EPA’s Climate Pollution Reduction Grants.
